school-skills-mental-maths.title: Mental Maths, Vedic-style Tricks & Abacus
school-skills-mental-maths.description: Fast, correct mental calculation: foundations, Vedic-style shortcuts (with honest notes on what they are), abacus concepts and percent estimation.

courses.title: Mental Maths Foundations
courses.summary: Compensation, doubling and halving, friendly numbers and quick checks that make everyday sums fast.
outcomes: Add and subtract by rounding and adjusting

scenes.text: Maya adds 47+38 for a stationery bill.
She rounds 38 to 40, adds, then takes 2 back.

steps.title: Compensation
steps.body: Round one number to a friendly number (10, 100), do the easy sum, and adjust. 47+38 = 47+40−2 = 85.

steps.title: Subtract
steps.body: 1000−648: 648 needs 352 to reach 1000. Answer 352.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Forgetting to put the adjustment back, or adjusting in the wrong direction. If you added extra, take it away.

steps.title: What this is
steps.body: These are calculation shortcuts based on ordinary arithmetic; they are tools to be understood, not magic. Always know why a trick works, and check with estimation.

scenes.text: Aman needs 56×25 runs in quick sums for a team table.
He remembers 25 is a quarter of 100.

steps.title: ×11 for two digits
steps.body: Add the digits and place in the middle: 36×11 → 3 (3+6) 6 = 396. If the sum exceeds 9, carry: 85 → 8 (13) 5 → 935.

scenes.text: Reeta gets 49×51=3,500 and feels something is wrong.
She estimates 50×50=2500.

steps.title: Estimate first
steps.body: Round numbers, compute roughly, then compare with your exact answer. Large gaps mean an error.

steps.title: Digit sums
steps.body: Casting out nines: a number's remainder mod 9 equals the remainder of its digit sum; use it to check multiplication.

lessons.title: What it is, and squares ending in 5

steps.title: What 'Vedic Maths' really is
steps.body: 'Vedic Mathematics' is a set of calculation shortcuts popularised by Bharati Krishna Tirthaji in a book published in 1965. The 16 'sutras' are not found in the ancient Vedas as such; they are a modern collection. The shortcuts themselves are valid arithmetic and are fun and useful, but they do not replace learning the standard methods.

quiz.q: Is Vedic Maths found word-for-word in the ancient Vedas?
options: Not as such; it is a modern collection

scenes.text: Ria needs 97×96 without a calculator.
She finds how far each is below 100.

steps.title: Method
steps.body: 97 is 3 below 100; 96 is 4 below. Cross-subtract: 97−4=93 (or 96−3). Multiply deficits: 3×4=12. Answer 93|12=9312.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: If the product of deficits has more than two digits, carry the extra into the left part.

scenes.text: Tara multiplies 23×14 in three small steps.
She multiplies vertically and crosswise.

steps.title: Steps
steps.body: Right: 3×4=12 (write 2 carry 1). Cross: 2×4+3×1=11, +1 = 12 (write 2 carry 1). Left: 2×1=2, +1 = 3 → 322.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Estimate 20×15=300; the answer 322 is sensible.

scenes.text: Is 2728 divisible by 11?
Alternate digit sum: 2−7+2−8=−11, a multiple of 11, so yes.

steps.title: Tests
steps.body: By 9: digit sum divisible by 9. By 11: alternating sum divisible by 11 (including 0).

statements.s: A number is divisible by 9 if its digit sum is divisible by 9.
Vedic tricks replace the standard methods.

steps.title: Make ten
steps.body: 6+7: add 10 on the next rod (+1 tens bead) and subtract 3 from the ones rod: leaves 3. Answer 13.

scenes.text: Aarav sees a scoreboard that shows 2, 5, 8, 11 and then goes blank.
He wonders what comes next and works out how the numbers grow.

steps.title: Find the rule
steps.body: Look at the **difference** between neighbours first. In 2, 5, 8, 11 each step adds 3. If differences are equal, the rule is 'add the same number'.

steps.title: Growing differences
steps.body: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25: differences are 3, 5, 7, 9. These are **square numbers**: 1×1, 2×2, 3×3 …

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Do not decide the rule from only two numbers. Check it on every pair before answering.

steps.title: Pair the ends
steps.body: Pair first and last: 1+100=101, 2+99=101 … There are 50 pairs, so the sum is 50×101=5050.

scenes.text: Two gears with 12 and 18 teeth start together at a marked tooth.
Ishaan wants to know when the marks meet again.

steps.title: HCF and LCM
steps.body: HCF(12,18)=6, LCM=36. Marks meet again after 36 teeth pass, i.e. 3 turns of the 12-gear and 2 of the 18-gear.

steps.title: Counting divisors
steps.body: 36=2²×3². Add 1 to each power and multiply: (2+1)(2+1)=9 divisors.

steps.title: LCM of 1–10
steps.body: Take the highest power of each prime: 2³×3²×5×7=2520.

scenes.text: Neha needs the last digit of 7 raised to the power 100.
She finds that last digits repeat in a cycle.

steps.title: Cycles
steps.body: Powers of 7 end in 7, 9, 3, 1 and then repeat every 4. 100 is a multiple of 4, so 7¹⁰⁰ ends in 1.

steps.title: Remainder
steps.body: 2¹⁰=1024; 1024=7×146+2, so the remainder is 2.

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Using the exponent itself, not the exponent's remainder after dividing by the cycle length.

scenes.text: A two-digit ticket number has digit sum 9; reversing it gives a number 27 more.
Aditi forms equations from the clues.

steps.title: Place value
steps.body: A number with digits a,b is 10a+b. Reversal is 10b+a. Difference =9(b−a)=27, so b−a=3.

steps.title: Solve
steps.body: a+b=9 and b−a=3 give a=3,b=6: the number is 36 (63−36=27 ✓).

steps.title: Three consecutive numbers
steps.body: If their sum is 72, middle number is 72÷3=24, so 23, 24, 25.
